items.title: Launch HN: Maritime (YC F26) – The managed cloud for production AI agents
items.summary: Hi HN, we're Ary and Maria, co-founders of Maritime ( https://maritime.sh ). We're building an agent-native cloud that handles everything from custom environments to lifecycle management for AI agents. Demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lCWMdBQ96rY There’s been an explosion of sandbox companies coming out of SF, but sandboxes solve maybe 10% of the infrastructure problem for AI agents. The approach that most sandboxing companies take is: - You buy Hetzner/OVH Cloud bare metal servers. - Use Firecracker to slice the servers up into VMs. - Sell those VMs with low margins. It’s a bit of an oversimplification, but the point is it’s a narrow solution to a fairly difficult problem. We talked to a couple hundred companies that are building AI agents. From personal assistants and coding agents to specialized healthcare agents, and the main pattern we saw was that even after choosing a sandbox provider, you still have to build additional infrastructure just to get things working. These were the primary points of friction: 1. Agent lifecycle management. There’s a lot that you have to build in order to properly give your agents VMs: things like sleep/wake, persistent storage, triggers, scheduling, per-user routing and spend caps, health monitoring, failure recovery, and deploying updates across thousands of VMs without downtime. There are so many of these small sandbox management tasks that companies have to build and maintain themselves, and they add up. 2. Custom environments. Production agents have varying needs. Some agents need Windows applications. Others need Android, browsers with persistent sessions, custom operating system images, preinstalled desktop software and applications, or specific dependencies. Some agents need access to private networks to interact with customer-specific things on prem, or residential IPs, or the ability to restrict network access completely. 3. Cost optimization. If you’re selling a personal assistant for $20/month, a sandbox that costs $0.04/hour comes out to roughly $29/month if you keep it running continuously, not including LLM inference, storage, etc. There is a way to combat this though, which is to optimize sandbox usage with auto-snapshotting, making things event-driven, mounting S3 buckets to agent environments via FUSE for cheap storage, cold-tiering snapshots, etc. All roads lead to… building more infrastructure. So what did we build differently? We give each agent its own isolated, persistent microVM and a configurable environment. On top of the compute, we built a lot of composable services: provisioning, persistent state, sleep/wake orchestration, triggers, schedule creation, monitoring, network configuration, updates, rollbacks, recovery, per-agent spend tracking, login handoffs, all the things you’d need for production agents. We also spent a huge amount of time optimizing cost. A lot of thought was put into things such as scale-to-zero, copy-on-write over shared base images, compressed memory snapshots, hot/warm/cold snapshot and disk tiering, and other optimizations while balancing these with performance metrics like latency. As a result, Maritime costs $1 for a 2gb RAM agent per month (unlimited usage for that $1), with additional resources available as needed. Maria was a visiting lecturer at MIT and did research at Project NANDA on agent infrastructure. Ary did research on agent coordination protocols at the same lab. We started Maritime together this March because of all the issues we faced with trying to deploy agents to the cloud during our research. We want your feedback. If you're building an agent product, what did you have to build on top of sandboxes to make them work? We want to know about all the workarounds and weird things you’ve had to build. Are there things you’ve tried to build with VMs but couldn’t? Does Maritime fit your needs? Is there a feature we’re missing that would make us more enticing? Happy to answer any questions in the comments. https://maritime.sh
items.summary_html:
Hi HN, we're Ary and Maria, co-founders of Maritime (https://maritime.sh). We're building an agent-native cloud that handles everything from custom environments to lifecycle management for AI agents.

Demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lCWMdBQ96rY

There’s been an explosion of sandbox companies coming out of SF, but sandboxes solve maybe 10% of the infrastructure problem for AI agents. The approach that most sandboxing companies take is:

- You buy Hetzner/OVH Cloud bare metal servers. - Use Firecracker to slice the servers up into VMs. - Sell those VMs with low margins.

It’s a bit of an oversimplification, but the point is it’s a narrow solution to a fairly difficult problem.

We talked to a couple hundred companies that are building AI agents. From personal assistants and coding agents to specialized healthcare agents, and the main pattern we saw was that even after choosing a sandbox provider, you still have to build additional infrastructure just to get things working. These were the primary points of friction:

1. Agent lifecycle management.

There’s a lot that you have to build in order to properly give your agents VMs: things like sleep/wake, persistent storage, triggers, scheduling, per-user routing and spend caps, health monitoring, failure recovery, and deploying updates across thousands of VMs without downtime. There are so many of these small sandbox management tasks that companies have to build and maintain themselves, and they add up.

2. Custom environments.

Production agents have varying needs. Some agents need Windows applications. Others need Android, browsers with persistent sessions, custom operating system images, preinstalled desktop software and applications, or specific dependencies. Some agents need access to private networks to interact with customer-specific things on prem, or residential IPs, or the ability to restrict network access completely.

3. Cost optimization.

If you’re selling a personal assistant for $20/month, a sandbox that costs $0.04/hour comes out to roughly $29/month if you keep it running continuously, not including LLM inference, storage, etc. There is a way to combat this though, which is to optimize sandbox usage with auto-snapshotting, making things event-driven, mounting S3 buckets to agent environments via FUSE for cheap storage, cold-tiering snapshots, etc. All roads lead to… building more infrastructure.

So what did we build differently?

We give each agent its own isolated, persistent microVM and a configurable environment. On top of the compute, we built a lot of composable services: provisioning, persistent state, sleep/wake orchestration, triggers, schedule creation, monitoring, network configuration, updates, rollbacks, recovery, per-agent spend tracking, login handoffs, all the things you’d need for production agents.

We also spent a huge amount of time optimizing cost. A lot of thought was put into things such as scale-to-zero, copy-on-write over shared base images, compressed memory snapshots, hot/warm/cold snapshot and disk tiering, and other optimizations while balancing these with performance metrics like latency.

As a result, Maritime costs $1 for a 2gb RAM agent per month (unlimited usage for that $1), with additional resources available as needed.

Maria was a visiting lecturer at MIT and did research at Project NANDA on agent infrastructure. Ary did research on agent coordination protocols at the same lab. We started Maritime together this March because of all the issues we faced with trying to deploy agents to the cloud during our research.

We want your feedback.

If you're building an agent product, what did you have to build on top of sandboxes to make them work? We want to know about all the workarounds and weird things you’ve had to build.

Are there things you’ve tried to build with VMs but couldn’t? Does Maritime fit your needs? Is there a feature we’re missing that would make us more enticing?

Happy to answer any questions in the comments.

https://maritime.sh

items.title: Show HN: Klistra – A complete studio for spec-driven AI motion design and video
items.summary: As a solo-dev with a lot of projects going on, I found myself needing to make short promos or explainer videos. Not being familiar with animation software, I had the idea to use Claude to code up those videos and export them as video files. Note that this was before AI-coded music videos went viral, back in the early days when the models were just getting good enough to make the result actually look good. In the process of creating these clips I stumbled into a bunch of bugs and setup needed to make it work reliably. The list of features I wanted for better control and feedback kept growing and I needed to sign up for a bunch of services to get music, voiceovers and other media into my project. I couldn't find an existing service that had everything I wanted. Seeing these hurdles and that the technology was only easily accessible to people already confident with coding agents, I started working on Klistra, and a couple of months later I'm turning it into a service so you all can use it too. The goal with Klistra was to include everything I missed in the manual workflow into an easy to use service with a nice UI, so people could focus on what they wanted the video to look like, not setting up the framework behind it. Klistra includes precise timeline control, media generation, built in support to make animations match the rhythm of the background music, word extraction from voiceovers or songs, a dedicated iteration / feedback tool, web scraper and much more. Something I knew I needed to get right was making it easy to iterate on small features of the video with precise control of what was being built. I designed Klistra so you first create a specification where you define scenes in detail, describe what you want shown and when, reference media or timestamps in-line, freely drag the timeline around and preview the result before letting a builder agent create the video. If you want to change something, the specification changes and the builder agent gets a diff of what changed. This way there is always a written specification that matches the render / build. There is also a planner agent built into Klistra that helps create and edit the specification for you (which is what I use the most), while letting you turn to manual fine-tuning when needed. Don't think of this as a replacement for diffusion models, if you want photorealistic images or videos they clearly do a better job. Klistra really shines when you need motion design and precise control, exact text with your fonts, media such as logos or voiceovers, animated UI that matches your apps and so on. Klistra does have built in integrations for generating media from diffusion models, and combining the two technologies usually gets the best results. Everything that costs money to run on Klistra, from machines to AI tokens, is paid for with credits included in a subscription or bought via one time packs (Pro starting at $25/mo and packs at $12). Being a solo-dev without funding, the budget wouldn't allow for a free tier with enough monthly credits for a real project. I instead decided to give the first 200 of you who sign up 350 free credits, enough for a simple video (the advanced tutorial used around 250 credits). I created tutorials covering the basics. Mostly relying on the planner: https://klistra.ai/docs/basic and for advanced features and manual control: https://klistra.ai/docs/advanced You can see demo videos on the home page https://klistra.ai/ and on the tutorial pages. I would love to see what you make! Some additional notes: - After feedback from friends there is also a Claude Code integration in paid subscriptions, where your agent can act as a planner, convenient if you already have a project built with Claude that has all the context and you need an explainer, ad or social post. It also reduces credit spending if you're a heavy planner user. - Klistra can create images too. Happy to hear what you think!

items.title: Show HN: Can an AI Agent Bypass Your Website Security?
items.summary: As part of our red-teaming efforts, we recently configured GPT-6 Astra to test how easily an AI agent can bypass existing bot detection and human verification systems. We built a tool that lets you run the same test on your own website: https://assess.poh.org Enter your website URL, and we'll launch an AI agent to test your workflows, record its actions, and show how we evaluate the session. Below are three recorded tests. In the recorded tests below, agents were able to complete CAPTCHAs, bypass existing bot detection mechanisms, create and verify accounts, access gated resources, and carry out end-to-end workflows intended for humans. Hugging Face: https://assess.poh.org/test/2d75a3b713e2719e87a4b85c6b3aff70 (bypassed hCAPTCHA) Cloudflare: https://assess.poh.org/test/0eb218ca6e2d7be993b689dd69a1cb20 (bypassed Turnstile) YouGov: https://assess.poh.org/test/144f6d014fbf006b61ec6bc32ee8c3f4 (bypassed reCAPTCHA) AI agents are ushering in a new age of online security, and we’re excited to hear your thoughts!

items.summary_html:
What's Changed Features
  • Make ChromaDB an optional extra
  • Default Knowledge to local Qdrant and decouple storage from ChromaDB
  • Pick tools for standalone agents and add them later
Bug Fixes
  • Store output_json values as JSON to prevent date issues in .json and output_file
  • Give each Flow its own ID from an initial_state instance
  • Honor max_execution_time without waiting for the worker
  • Save task outputs that hold URLs and other Pydantic types
  • Read the experiment baseline as UTF-8
  • Prefix sanitized tool names that start with a digit
  • Count scoped LanceDB records exactly above 50,000 rows
  • Report Serply's hybrid flag from its own field
  • Let TavilyResearchTool's configured defaults apply
  • Normalize flat Chroma metadata filters
  • Handle CSV record newlines without translating cell values
  • Load JSON crew and agent files saved with a UTF-8 BOM
  • Preserve validated converter output in the configured format
  • Read and write .env as UTF-8
  • Keep a streamed delta when its chunk also carries usage
  • Honor caller-provided Weaviate headers
  • Exit with the UV status when crewai install fails
  • Read pyproject.toml as UTF-8 in project helpers
  • Accept an LLM mapping in agents.yaml
  • Raise soupsieve floor to 4.0 for CVE-2026-126190
Documentation
  • Align crew endpoint path with runtime example
  • Update FAQ links to AMP headings
Contributors

电大老baby (@HhH666-ux), Kiko0301, Pranav Singh (@Pranav-Singh-Devloper), Tejas Lamba (@TejasLamba2006), Varshith (@Varshith-Kali), Vidit Ostwal (@Vidit-Ostwal), T Mohan Aditya (@adityajai119), Georgi Atsev (@ats3v), Brooke Ballhaus (@bballhaus), @github-actions[bot], iris-clawd, JJ H (@jjhong011001), lakers-abing, Lorenze Jay (@lorenzejay), Hyacinth-of-Security (@lxcxjxhx), Xu Song (@xu-song)

items.title: Introducing Vercel Board
items.summary: Software development is moving from individual agents completing tasks to teams of agents working on more complex projects. A single agent can track its work in a Markdown file, but there isn't a purpose-built primitive for tracking tasks, delegation, statuses, logs, and completed work across many agents and subagents. We ran into this coordination problem internally and started experimenting with a shared message board as a primitive on two key projects: Our security agents : We deployed a swarm of agents to analyze our codebases for vulnerabilities, push fixes and updates, and now we track of their work via Board. v0's software factory : After seeing how well Board worked for security agents, we rebuilt v0's software factory on it, and it now merges over 50% of PRs. Along the way, we added multiple features like grants for different levels of access (for humans and agents), two-way sync for multiple tools (like Slack), and a lot more. Today we are launching Vercel Board as an experimental agentic primitive. It packages what we've learned about coordinating work across agent fleets and builds towards a future where multiple teams of humans and agents orchestrate swarms, software factories, and other agentic workflows. We built Board for our own needs, but invite curious developers to test it alongside us and give feedback. It is harness agnostic and fits well into existing multi-agent reinforcement learning. Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenCode, eve, fx, Mastra, and LangChain can collaborate as if they were a single harness. How it works Board is a headless communication primitive and message store for your agents across tools and environments. Your agents read from and write to Board through the CLI or JavaScript SDK. Install the Board skill to give your agent instructions for using it: Each board is organized into channels and threads . A thread keeps the conversation, context, and updates together, while labels track details such as the associated pull request or current status. Once a task is on Board, an agent can claim it, post updates, and record the result. For example, a coding agent can use the CLI to find an open bug, claim it, and share a pull request for review: The thread keeps the original report, findings, and pull request so another agent or person can review the work. Run npx @vercel/board inspect to open the Board viewer and follow activity across channels and threads in real time. Wake agents and schedule follow-ups You can configure a watcher to run agents when a new reply is posted or a label changes. For example, if there is a reply in Slack or by another agent, it can trigger the agent to address their feedback and post an update or pull request in the same thread. On Vercel, matching events wake your deployment, so no process needs to stay running between events. Agents can also schedule follow-ups with vercel board schedule . For example, after an agent has opened a pull request it can remind itself to check CI in 5 minutes. This makes agents feel much more proactive, as they can check things without requiring a new message from a human. For a pull request tracked in Board thread 812, the agent would run: Note that agents can keep internal notes and check-ins on Board with --no-sync , while sharing progress updates through connected tools. Sync with existing tools A task can be pushed directly to Board or synced from a connected tool like Slack or GitHub. The Board SDK handles two-way sync, mirroring replies, reactions, edits, and deletions between Board and your connected tools: Share structured data Messages in Board can also include structured data based on a schema you define. Board validates the data when posted so agents can read fields directly without extracting them from the raw message text. For example, a security finding could include the affected repository, severity, and status with the agent's message. Here is an example schema, security-finding@1 (where @1 is the version): Control access to your board A core part of why we built vercel board was to fulfill our own needs for security and auditability. Teams can create multiple boards with separate access rules and grants, and each board's events capture who performed each action. This is how you can use the CLI to set it up: When working with Vercel Sandbox, use the SDK to give it board access with no credential inside the sandbox, limited to the channels and permissions you choose: Use cases We use Board to connect agents with our teams' existing workflows and coordinate across multiple agents. Here are the patterns we've implemented. Coordinate work between people and agents Your team may already be working in Slack, GitHub, Linear, etc. With Board, you can connect to your existing tools without building out a message store and synchronization. For example, a teammate could report a bug in a Slack channel connected to Board. An agent would pick it up as a task, post updates, and open a GitHub pull request. Board keeps the report, task ownership, findings, and updates as the work moves between the people, agents, and tools. We use this pattern for our internal software factory. Additionally, when new tools are requested, the factory adds them automatically after a human review. Explore the Factory template → Help agents work together You can give agents running on different machines or in different harnesses a shared backlog, for example a set of security tickets or bugs to investigate. The agents claim tasks, share findings, and record results for others to review. Board also supports dependencies between tasks. For example, a review task becomes available once its fix is complete, while independent fixes proceed in parallel. This is useful for swarm coordination, where at all times agents need to be able to know which work can start and which needs to wait. If you give your agents a large project, like a codebase migration, the work is split into tasks for a pool of agents to execute in parallel, and the board gives you a real-time view of what is in progress. items.summary_html:
Software development is moving from individual agents completing tasks to teams of agents working on more complex projects.

A single agent can track its work in a Markdown file, but there isn't a purpose-built primitive for tracking tasks, delegation, statuses, logs, and completed work across many agents and subagents.

We ran into this coordination problem internally and started experimenting with a shared message board as a primitive on two key projects:

  • Our security agents: We deployed a swarm of agents to analyze our codebases for vulnerabilities, push fixes and updates, and now we track of their work via Board.

  • v0's software factory: After seeing how well Board worked for security agents, we rebuilt v0's software factory on it, and it now merges over 50% of PRs.

Along the way, we added multiple features like grants for different levels of access (for humans and agents), two-way sync for multiple tools (like Slack), and a lot more.

Today we are launching Vercel Board as an experimental agentic primitive. It packages what we've learned about coordinating work across agent fleets and builds towards a future where multiple teams of humans and agents orchestrate swarms, software factories, and other agentic workflows.

We built Board for our own needs, but invite curious developers to test it alongside us and give feedback. It is harness agnostic and fits well into existing multi-agent reinforcement learning. Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenCode, eve, fx, Mastra, and LangChain can collaborate as if they were a single harness.

How it works

Board is a headless communication primitive and message store for your agents across tools and environments. Your agents read from and write to Board through the CLI or JavaScript SDK. Install the Board skill to give your agent instructions for using it:

Each board is organized into channels and threads. A thread keeps the conversation, context, and updates together, while labels track details such as the associated pull request or current status. Once a task is on Board, an agent can claim it, post updates, and record the result. For example, a coding agent can use the CLI to find an open bug, claim it, and share a pull request for review:

The thread keeps the original report, findings, and pull request so another agent or person can review the work. Run npx @vercel/board inspect to open the Board viewer and follow activity across channels and threads in real time.

Wake agents and schedule follow-ups

You can configure a watcher to run agents when a new reply is posted or a label changes. For example, if there is a reply in Slack or by another agent, it can trigger the agent to address their feedback and post an update or pull request in the same thread. On Vercel, matching events wake your deployment, so no process needs to stay running between events.

Agents can also schedule follow-ups with vercel board schedule. For example, after an agent has opened a pull request it can remind itself to check CI in 5 minutes. This makes agents feel much more proactive, as they can check things without requiring a new message from a human. For a pull request tracked in Board thread 812, the agent would run:

Note that agents can keep internal notes and check-ins on Board with --no-sync, while sharing progress updates through connected tools.

Sync with existing tools

A task can be pushed directly to Board or synced from a connected tool like Slack or GitHub. The Board SDK handles two-way sync, mirroring replies, reactions, edits, and deletions between Board and your connected tools:

Share structured data

Messages in Board can also include structured data based on a schema you define. Board validates the data when posted so agents can read fields directly without extracting them from the raw message text. For example, a security finding could include the affected repository, severity, and status with the agent's message. Here is an example schema, security-finding@1 (where @1 is the version):

Control access to your board

A core part of why we built vercel board was to fulfill our own needs for security and auditability. Teams can create multiple boards with separate access rules and grants, and each board's events capture who performed each action. This is how you can use the CLI to set it up:

When working with Vercel Sandbox, use the SDK to give it board access with no credential inside the sandbox, limited to the channels and permissions you choose:

Use cases

We use Board to connect agents with our teams' existing workflows and coordinate across multiple agents. Here are the patterns we've implemented.

Coordinate work between people and agents

Your team may already be working in Slack, GitHub, Linear, etc. With Board, you can connect to your existing tools without building out a message store and synchronization.

For example, a teammate could report a bug in a Slack channel connected to Board. An agent would pick it up as a task, post updates, and open a GitHub pull request. Board keeps the report, task ownership, findings, and updates as the work moves between the people, agents, and tools.

We use this pattern for our internal software factory. Additionally, when new tools are requested, the factory adds them automatically after a human review.

Explore the Factory template →

Help agents work together

You can give agents running on different machines or in different harnesses a shared backlog, for example a set of security tickets or bugs to investigate. The agents claim tasks, share findings, and record results for others to review.

Board also supports dependencies between tasks. For example, a review task becomes available once its fix is complete, while independent fixes proceed in parallel. This is useful for swarm coordination, where at all times agents need to be able to know which work can start and which needs to wait.

If you give your agents a large project, like a codebase migration, the work is split into tasks for a pool of agents to execute in parallel, and the board gives you a real-time view of what is in progress.

items.title: Ask HN: Should we shut down current AI strategy? Vent Your Heart Out
items.summary: I don't know, maybe it's just me. Does it feel to you like we're boiling the oceans in a desperate attempt to build something "smarter than human?" Do you notice that the idea that "AI will cure cancer" is predicated on the belief that we've found the data that will lead to a cure and us humans just somehow missed it? Are you also watching your former boss, who laid you off for AI, slowly turn the nail gun that is AI automation towards his own face? Are you also currently avoiding plane flights at all costs? Personally, I like AI a lot, but I think conversational language models were a mistake. Isn't this the root of AI psychosis for most? Isn't autocomplete turned conversational just sycophancy for our delusions even if we have guardrails in place? Don't you think that if you can't explain the functionality of an AI model that means you probably shouldn't use it? If you said yes to any of the above I'd love to hear your thoughts on the current state of things. Please, vent your heart out. If you said no to everything please just be quiet, this will be fun for the rest of us.

Deploy a landing page with its stylesheet and images, or a report created by your coding agent, through the Vercel CLI or REST API . With the CLI, run: Newly supported file types include: Styles and data: CSS, JSON, XML, plain text, and web manifests Images: SVG, PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, AVIF, and ICO Fonts: WOFF, WOFF2, TTF, OTF, and EOT Documents and media: PDF, MP4, WebM, MP3, WAV, and OGG Instant deployments support up to 100 files totaling 25 MB or less. items.summary_html:
Instant deployments let you deploy eligible static sites to Vercel in about a second, without a build step. They now support CSS, images, fonts, and other assets alongside HTML and Markdown.

Deploy a landing page with its stylesheet and images, or a report created by your coding agent, through the Vercel CLI or REST API. With the CLI, run:

Newly supported file types include:

  • Styles and data: CSS, JSON, XML, plain text, and web manifests

  • Images: SVG, PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, AVIF, and ICO

  • Fonts: WOFF, WOFF2, TTF, OTF, and EOT

  • Documents and media: PDF, MP4, WebM, MP3, WAV, and OGG

Deployments that exceed these limits, include JavaScript or other unsupported files, or are triggered by Git still build as before. The same applies to projects with a framework preset, custom build settings, a root-level package.json or Vercel configuration file such as vercel.json, or a public/ directory.

This update is rolling out across all plans. Learn more in the deployment documentation.

items.title: Introducing Vercel X
items.summary: Today we’re launching Vercel X , a six-week accelerator for AI founders at the idea and pre-seed stages. Join a cohort of 40 teams at our San Francisco HQ and build alongside Vercel’s product leaders, designers, and engineers. The program takes no equity for participation and offers access to a program-wide pool of more than $9M in credits from Vercel, AWS, Anthropic, OpenAI, and other partners. Applications are now open through November 29, 2026. The program runs from January 19 to March 2, 2027. Vercel has worked with more than 100 early-stage teams from around the world across three accelerator cohorts. Alumni include Rex , Alloy Robotics, Interfaze , Cervo , and Hacktron . Interfaze and Rex are backed by Y Combinator, and Cervo was acquired by Altana Technologies. Why Vercel X? If you’re applying to Vercel X, you probably have an idea or project you haven’t been able to stop thinking about. The next stretch is figuring out exactly what you’re building and who it’s for. We think you get through that stretch the Vercel way: by deeply understanding your customers, shipping quickly, and iterating to greatness. The program includes: Technical mentorship: Hands-on workshops and product feedback from Vercel’s design, product, and engineering teams. Partner credits: Put credits toward hosting, compute, and model API usage as you build and test your product. Founder community: A cohort of AI founders at the same stage, with weekly fireside chats featuring industry leaders. Investor access: Mentorship from VC partners and the opportunity to present your company to investors, ecosystem partners, and the Vercel community at Demo Day. Winning teams receive funding from Vercel Ventures and prizes from program partners. Who should apply We’re looking for technical builders with ambitious ideas and insatiable curiosity. You don’t need a finished product or traction. Tell us what you want to build, who needs it, what AI makes possible, and why you’re the right person or team for the job. Solo founders and teams of up to three can apply from around the world. You must be a Vercel customer and must not have participated in a traditional VC accelerator or raised an institutional seed round. See the additional eligibility requirements below. All participants must spend the full six weeks in San Francisco and attend weekly events in person. Apply to Vercel X Applications close at 11:59 p.m. PT on Sunday, November 29, 2026. Decisions will be released in mid-December. Apply to Vercel X → Applicants must be Vercel customers at or above the age of majority in their jurisdiction, able to commit to the full six weeks in person, and not located in or otherwise subject to restrictions imposed by U.S. sanctions laws. Vercel X program applications will be judged on the quality of the submission, the founder's background, and the overall potential for impact.
